subject: English
topic: Active and Passive Voice — Advanced Conversion and Error Identification for SSC CGL (W13 B1)

questions.stem: Identify the CORRECT passive form of: 'They have been building the dam for three years.'

options.option_text: The dam has been built for three years by them.
The dam has been being built for three years by them.
The dam was being built for three years by them.
The dam had been built for three years by them.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Active: 'have been building' = present perfect continuous. Passive of present perfect continuous: have/has + been + being + past participle. 'The dam HAS BEEN BEING BUILT for three years by them.' Note: this form is grammatically correct but rarely used in practice — which is exactly why SSC tests it. Trap: 'has been built' = present perfect simple passive (for completed action, not continuous); 'was being built' = past continuous passive (wrong tense: active uses HAVE not WAS).

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly converts 'Let the work be completed by Friday' to active voice?

options.option_text: Complete the work by Friday.
The work should be completed by Friday.
We let the work complete by Friday.
You are let to complete the work by Friday.

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Let + object + be + past participle' (passive imperative) → Active imperative: 'Complete the work by Friday.' The passive imperative 'Let it be done' converts to the direct command 'Do it.' The subject ('you') is implied. Trap: 'The work should be completed' = a suggestion/modal, not the direct active command; 'We let the work complete' = uses 'let' as 'allow' (different sense).

questions.stem: Choose the CORRECT passive voice of: 'Someone has stolen my wallet.'

options.option_text: My wallet was stolen by someone.
My wallet had been stolen.
My wallet has been stolen.
My wallet was being stolen.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Active: 'has stolen' = present perfect. Passive of present perfect: has/have + been + past participle = 'has been stolen'. Agent: 'someone' is vague and dropped in passive (standard practice — do not write 'by someone'). Result: 'My wallet has been stolen.' Trap: 'was stolen' = simple past passive (tense mismatch — active is present perfect, not simple past); 'had been stolen' = past perfect passive (wrong tense).

questions.stem: Convert to passive voice: 'People say that honesty is the best policy.'

options.option_text: Honesty is said to be the best policy.
It is saying that honesty is the best policy.
Honesty was said to be the best policy by people.
Honesty has been said to be the best policy.

questions.explanation: A is correct. When 'people say/think/believe/know/consider' has a that-clause object, passive can be formed two ways: (1) It + is + said + that-clause: 'It is said that honesty is the best policy.' (2) Subject of that-clause + is + said + to-infinitive: 'Honesty is said TO BE the best policy.' Both are correct but option A matches form (2). Note: 'by people' is dropped (vague agent). Trap: 'was said' = past tense (active uses present 'say'); 'has been said' = present perfect (mismatch).

questions.stem: Which passive voice conversion is INCORRECT?

options.option_text: Active: 'She knows the answer.' → Passive: 'The answer is known by her.'
Active: 'He laughed at the joke.' → Passive: 'The joke was laughed at by him.'
Active: 'The news surprised me.' → Passive: 'I was surprised by the news.'
Active: 'She belongs to a wealthy family.' → Passive: 'A wealthy family is belonged to by her.'

questions.explanation: D is correct — D is the INCORRECT conversion. 'Belong to' is a STATIVE VERB (state of possession/relationship) and cannot be converted to passive voice. Stative verbs (resemble, contain, belong, consist, lack, possess, own) do not have passive forms. You cannot say 'A wealthy family is belonged to by her.' Trap: A is correct (stative 'know' CAN form passive in this case as it describes the state of knowledge); B is correct (phrasal verb 'laugh at' → 'was laughed at' — preposition keeps with verb in passive); C is correct (emotional/causative verbs like 'surprise', 'please', 'interest' have passive forms).

questions.stem: Convert to active voice: 'The meeting is being attended by all senior officials.'

options.option_text: All senior officials are attending the meeting.
All senior officials attend the meeting.
All senior officials have attended the meeting.
All senior officials were attending the meeting.

questions.explanation: A is correct. Passive: 'is being attended' = present continuous passive. Active: 'is/are + verb-ing' = present continuous. Subject = 'all senior officials' (plural) → 'are attending'. Result: 'All senior officials ARE ATTENDING the meeting.' Trap: 'attend' = simple present (drops the continuous aspect: 'is being' → 'are -ing'); 'were attending' = past continuous (wrong tense: 'is being' is present, not past).

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive voice of the imperative: 'Please post this letter.'

options.option_text: This letter is requested to be posted.
You are requested to post this letter.
This letter was posted please.
This letter should have been posted.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Passive of a POLITE imperative (with 'please'): 'You are requested to + base verb + object.' The structure preserves the polite request. 'Please post this letter' → 'You are requested to post this letter.' The imperative passive uses 'You are requested/advised/ordered to...' — the 'you' (implied subject in the active imperative) becomes explicit in the passive. Trap: 'This letter is requested to be posted' = grammatically awkward (letter cannot be 'requested'); 'should have been posted' = past modal — completely wrong tense.

questions.stem: Convert to passive voice: 'The manager gave the employee a promotion.'

options.option_text: A promotion was given to the employee by the manager.
The employee was given a promotion by the manager.
Both A and B are correct passive transformations.
A promotion has been given to the employee.

questions.explanation: C is correct. When an active sentence has both DIRECT OBJECT (DO) and INDIRECT OBJECT (IO), TWO passive forms are possible: (1) IO becomes subject: 'The employee (IO) was given a promotion (DO) by the manager.' (2) DO becomes subject: 'A promotion (DO) was given to the employee (IO) by the manager.' Both are grammatically correct. This is one of the most frequently tested passive rules in SSC — the double-object passive. Trap: Both A and B are correct; choosing only one misses half the rule.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence that uses passive voice INCORRECTLY:

options.option_text: Hindi is spoken by millions of people.
The bridge is being constructed since last year.
The results will be declared by the board tomorrow.
The evidence had been tampered with before the trial.

questions.explanation: B is correct — B is INCORRECT. 'Is being constructed since last year' uses PRESENT CONTINUOUS PASSIVE with 'since' — but 'since' requires PRESENT PERFECT (not continuous) because it marks the start of an ongoing action extending to now. Correct: 'The bridge HAS BEEN BEING CONSTRUCTED since last year' (present perfect continuous passive) or more naturally 'The bridge has been under construction since last year.' The error: mixing present continuous ('is being') with a 'since' time marker that requires present perfect. Trap: A, C, D are all grammatically correct passive sentences.

questions.stem: Convert to active voice: 'It is expected that the project will be completed by December.'

options.option_text: We expect the project to be completed by December.
People expect that the project will be completed by December.
The project is expected to be completed by December.
They expect that the project will be completed by December.

questions.explanation: D is correct. 'It is expected that...' is a passive construction with an impersonal subject 'It'. Converting to active: the passive agent is 'they' (unspecified people — the same transformation as 'It is said that people say that'). Active: 'They expect that the project will be completed by December.' Note: 'will be completed' remains as the inner clause is itself passive. Trap: 'We expect' = changes unspecified 'they' to specific 'we'; 'The project is expected to be completed' = changes to another passive form (not active); 'People expect' = acceptable but 'they expect' is the standard active transformation of impersonal passive 'it is expected'.
